definition: The challenge and set of techniques for successfully transferring behaviors or policies learned in a simulated environment to work reliably in the real world.
details: Sim-to-real transfer is a significant challenge in robotics, since simulations inevitably differ from real-world physics and sensor characteristics in ways that can cause policies trained purely in simulation to fail when deployed on real hardware.

explainer.lead: Policies trained in simulation often break on real hardware because simulated physics and sensors never match reality exactly. Sim-to-real transfer is the set of techniques that closes that gap so learned behaviours survive deployment.

tiers.eli5: Like learning to ride a bike in a video game and then trying on a real one — the game leaves out wind, bumps and wobble, so you need tricks to make the skills carry over.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers randomise simulation parameters such as friction, mass and sensor noise so the policy sees many variants and generalises. A common pitfall is tuning randomisation too narrowly, which leaves the policy brittle to the real mismatch it never saw.
tiers.paperLevel: Formally, a policy is trained to maximise expected return under a distribution of simulated dynamics, hoping it also performs well under the real dynamics; no guarantee holds unless the real environment is covered by that distribution.

explainer.example: A walking robot trained with randomised ground friction and motor delays in simulation is then deployed and keeps its balance on a real floor.
